# The leg, ankle, and foot

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Rheumatology and immunology > Basics of rheumatology > The leg, ankle, and foot*

[Original Article Link](/library/p60LNS)

---

## Summary

The lower extremity consists of the hip, <u>thigh, knee, and popliteal fossa</u>, as well as the leg (crus), ankle, and foot. The leg (crus) extends from the knee to the ankle and contains the <u>tibia</u> and <u>fibula</u>. The <u>tarsal bones</u> include the <u>calcaneus</u>, <u>talus</u>, <u>cuboid</u>, <u>navicular bones</u>, and the <u>medial</u>, middle, and <u>lateral</u> <u>cuneiform bones</u>. The <u>ankle joint</u> (talocrural <u>joint</u>) is formed by the articulation of the <u>talus</u> with the <u>tibia</u> and <u>fibula</u>. The <u>talus</u> also articulates with the <u>calcaneus</u> inferiorly forming the subtalar <u>joint</u> and with the <u>navicular</u> anteriorly forming the talonavicular <u>joint</u>. The foot consists of 5 <u>metatarsal</u> bones, the <u>phalanges</u>, metatarsophalangeal (<u>MTP</u>), and interphalangeal (IP) <u>joints</u>. The foot has one transverse and two longitudinal arches that help distribute body weight. The leg (crus) has an <u>anterior</u>, <u>posterior</u>, and <u>lateral</u> compartment. The <u>anterior</u> compartment (extensor compartment), which is innervated by the <u>peroneal nerve</u>, contains muscles involved in ankle <u>dorsiflexion</u> and <u>foot eversion</u>. The <u>posterior</u> compartment (flexor compartment), which is innervated by the <u>tibial nerve</u>, contains muscles involved in ankle <u>plantarflexion</u>, <u>foot inversion</u>, and knee <u>flexion</u>. The <u>lateral</u> compartment (peroneal or fibular compartment), which is innervated by the <u>superficial peroneal nerve</u>, contains muscles involved in <u>foot eversion</u> and ankle <u>plantarflexion</u>. The <u>intrinsic muscles of the foot</u> are responsible for fine movements of the foot, which include <u>flexion</u> and extension at the <u>MTP</u> and <u>IP joints</u> as well as <u>abduction</u> and <u>adduction</u> of toes. The leg, ankle, and foot are <u>perfused</u> by the <u>anterior</u> and <u>posterior tibial arteries</u>, <u>fibular artery</u>, and their branches. These are drained by <u>superficial</u> (<u>great saphenous vein</u>, <u>small saphenous vein</u>) and <u>deep veins</u> (<u>anterior tibial vein</u>, <u>posterior tibial vein</u>, <u>fibular vein</u>).

---

## Bones and joints

### Bones of the leg




#### Tibia




<u>Medial</u> bone of the leg




* Important landmarks

* Tibial condyles: horizontal upper surface of the <u>tibia</u> with <u>medial</u> and <u>lateral</u> depressions that articulate with the femoral condyles

* Tibial tuberosity

* A rough triangular area on the <u>anterior</u> aspect of the <u>tibia</u>, where the condyles merge

* Site of attachment of the <u>patellar tendon</u>

* Clinical significance: <u>Osgood Schlatter disease</u>

* Shaft: has 3 surfaces (<u>anterior</u>, <u>lateral</u>, and <u>posterior</u>)

* Medial malleolus: inferomedial projection of the <u>distal</u> end of the <u>tibia</u>

* Function

* <u>Weight-bearing</u> bone

* Articulates superiorly with the femoral condyles to form <u>the knee joint</u>

* Articulates with the <u>talus</u> to form a portion of the <u>ankle joint</u>

* Articulates with the <u>fibula</u> proximally and distally

* Site of attachment of lower extremity muscles





![Ventral, dorsal, and lateral view of the tibia](media/oksyw127ukp1kdbx27yoggjv.jpg)

Ventral, dorsal, and lateral view of the tibia




#### Fibula




<u>Lateral</u> bone of the leg; non-weight bearing




* Important landmarks

* Head

* Site of attachment of the <u>lateral collateral ligament</u> of the knee and the <u>biceps femoris</u> muscle

* A component of the <u>proximal</u> tibiofibular <u>joint</u>

* Neck

* A constriction between the head and the shaft of the <u>fibula</u>

* <u>Common peroneal nerve</u> wraps around on the neck of the <u>fibula</u>

* Shaft: has 3 surfaces (<u>anterior</u>, <u>lateral</u>, and <u>posterior</u>)

* Lateral malleolus: inferolateral projection of the <u>distal</u> end of the <u>fibula</u>

* Function

* Articulates with the <u>talus</u> to form a portion of the <u>ankle joint</u>

* Site of attachment of lower extremity muscles





![Ventral, dorsal, and medial view of the fibula](media/axnviz949rudew796tp0ubqa.jpg)

Ventral, dorsal, and medial view of the fibula




### <u>Joints</u> of the leg




#### Tibiofibular <u>joints</u>




* <u>Proximal</u> tibiofibular <u>joint</u>: <u>synovial joint</u> between the head of the <u>fibula</u> and the <u>lateral</u> tibial condyle

* <u>Distal</u> tibiofibular <u>joint</u>: <u>fibrous joint</u> (<u>syndesmosis</u>) between the <u>distal</u> ends of the <u>tibia</u> and <u>fibula</u>





#### Interosseous membrane of the leg




Fibrous <u>connective tissue</u> that extends between the <u>medial</u> border of the <u>fibula</u> and the <u>lateral</u> border of the <u>tibia</u>




* Important landmark: A notch at the superior end permits the <u>anterior</u> tibial vessels to enter the <u>anterior compartment of the leg</u>.

* Function

* Stabilizes the tibiofibular <u>joints</u>

* Site of attachment of numerous <u>leg muscles</u>





### Bones of the ankle (tarsal bones)




Seven <u>tarsal bones</u> make up the <u>ankle joint</u>




| Characteristics of <u>tarsal bones</u> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <u>Tarsal bones</u> | Anatomy | Function |
| Talus | <br><br>* Most superior tarsal bone<br><br>* Has a groove for the interosseous <u>ligaments</u><br><br>* Has a groove for the <u>tendon</u> of the <u>flexor hallucis longus</u><br><br>* Articulations<br><br>* Superior: with the <u>tibia</u> and <u>fibula</u> to form the <u>ankle joint</u><br><br>* Inferior: with the <u>calcaneus</u> (subtalar <u>joint</u>)<br><br>* Anteriorly: with the <u>navicular</u> (talonavicular <u>joint</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Transmits bodyweight from the <u>tibia</u> to the <u>calcaneus</u><br><br>* Forms part of the <u>medial</u> longitudinal arch of the foot<br><br><br> |
| <br>Calcaneus  <br> | <br><br>* Located beneath the <u>talus</u> bone<br><br>* Has an inferior groove for the <u>tendon</u> of the <u>flexor hallucis longus</u><br><br>* Articulations<br><br>* Superior: <u>talus</u><br><br>* <u>Anterior</u>: <u>cuboid</u> bone (calcaneocuboid <u>joint</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Forms the heel of the foot and transmits bodyweight from the <u>talus</u> to the ground<br><br>* Site of attachment for the <u>Achilles tendon</u><br><br><br> |
| Navicular | <br><br>* Boat-shaped bone located medially in the <u>proximal</u> foot<br><br>* Articulations<br><br>* <u>Posterior</u>: <u>talus</u><br><br>* <u>Anterior</u>: the three <u>cuneiform bones</u><br><br>* <u>Lateral</u>: <u>cuboid</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Site of attachment to the <u>tibialis posterior</u> <u>tendon</u><br><br> |
| Cuneiform | <br><br>* 3 wedge-shaped bones<br><br>* <u>Medial</u> <u>cuneiform</u><br><br>* Intermediate <u>cuneiform</u><br><br>* <u>Lateral</u> <u>cuneiform</u><br><br>* Articulations<br><br>* <u>Posterior</u>: <u>navicular bone</u><br><br>* <u>Anterior</u>: 1<sup>st</sup>–3<sup>rd</sup> <u>metatarsal</u> bones, respectively<br><br><br> | <br>* Forms part of the <u>proximal</u> transverse and <u>medial</u> longitudinal arches of the foot<br><br> |
| Cuboid | <br><br>* Most <u>lateral</u> tarsal bone<br><br>* Contains a groove for the <u>tendon</u> of the <u>fibularis longus</u> (<u>peroneus longus</u>) muscle<br><br>* Articulations<br><br>* <u>Anterior</u>: 4<sup>th</sup> <u>metatarsal</u> bone<br><br>* Anterolateral: 5<sup>th</sup> <u>metatarsal</u> bone<br><br>* <u>Posterior</u>: <u>calcaneus</u><br><br>* <u>Medial</u>: <u>lateral</u> <u>cuneiform</u> and the <u>cuboid</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Forms part of the <u>lateral</u> longitudinal arch of the foot<br><br> |

### Ankle joint




* Type: synovial <u>hinge joint</u>

* Components: the <u>talus</u> with the <u>tibia</u> and <u>fibula</u>

* <u>Ligaments</u>

* <u>Medial</u> <u>ligament</u> (<u>deltoid ligament</u>) 

* Extends from the <u>medial malleolus</u> to the <u>medial</u> <u>tarsal bones</u>

* Composed by the <u>anterior</u> tibiotalar <u>ligament</u>, tibiocalcaneal <u>ligament</u>, <u>posterior</u> tibiotalar <u>ligament</u>, and tibionavicular <u>ligament</u>

* Prevents excessive ankle <u>eversion</u>

* <u>Lateral</u> <u>ligament</u> 

* Extends from the <u>lateral malleolus</u> to the <u>talus</u> and <u>calcaneus</u>

* Composed by the <u>anterior</u> talofibular <u>ligament</u>, <u>posterior</u> talofibular <u>ligament</u>, and calcaneofibular <u>ligament</u>

* Prevents excessive ankle <u>inversion</u>

* Commonly injured in <u>sports injuries</u> (<u>inversion</u> injury)

* Movements (uniaxial) 

* <u>Flexion</u> (plantarflexion)

* Extension (dorsiflexion)

### Bones and <u>joints</u> of the foot




* Metatarsal bones

* There are five <u>metatarsal bones</u> that are located <u>distal</u> to the <u>tarsal bones</u>.

* Each has a base that articulates with the <u>tarsal bones</u> (tarsometatarsal <u>joints</u>), a head that articulates with the <u>proximal</u> <u>phalanges</u> (<u>metatarsophalangeal joints</u>), and a shaft in between.

* <u>Phalanges</u>

* Small <u>long bones</u> of the toes

* Each toe has three <u>phalanges</u>, except the <u>hallux</u>, which only has two.

* Metatarsophalangeal joints (<u>MTP joints</u>)

* <u>Medial</u> 3 tarsophalangeal <u>joints</u>: between the <u>medial</u> 3 <u>proximal</u> <u>phalanges</u> and the 3 <u>cuneiform bones</u>

* <u>Lateral</u> 2 tarsophalangeal <u>joints</u>: between the <u>lateral</u> 2 <u>proximal</u> <u>phalanges</u> and the <u>cuboid</u>

* <u>Interphalangeal joints</u>

* The <u>lateral</u> 4 toes have <u>proximal</u> and <u>distal interphalangeal joints</u>.

* The <u>hallux</u> only has one <u>interphalangeal joint</u>.

### Arches of the foot




There are 3 arches in the foot: two longitudinal and one transverse.




* Function

* Distribute the body weight

* Act like springs and <u>shock</u> absorbers while running and walking

* Clinical significance

* <u>Pes cavus</u>

* <u>Pes planus</u>





| Characteristics of foot arches |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Arch | Formed by | Supporting structures |
| <u>Medial</u> longitudinal arch | <br><br>* <u>Calcaneus</u><br><br>* <u>Talus</u><br><br>* <u>Navicular</u><br><br>* 3 <u>cuneiforms</u><br><br>* <u>Medial</u> 3 <u>metatarsals</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Tibialis anterior</u><br><br>* <u>Tibialis posterior</u><br><br>* <u>Fibularis longus</u><br><br>* <u>Flexor digitorum longus</u><br><br>* Flexor hallucis<br><br>* <u>Intrinsic muscles of the foot</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Lateral</u> longitudinal arch | <br><br>* <u>Calcaneus</u><br><br>* <u>Cuboid</u><br><br>* 4<sup>th</sup> and 5<sup>th</sup> <u>metatarsals</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Fibularis longus</u><br><br>* <u>Flexor digitorum longus</u><br><br>* <u>Intrinsic muscles of the foot</u><br><br>* Reinforced by the <u>plantar</u> calcaneocuboid and the long <u>plantar</u> <u>ligaments</u><br><br><br> |
| Transverse arch | <br><br>* Bases of the 5 <u>metatarsals</u><br><br>* <u>Cuboid</u><br><br>* 3 <u>cuneiforms</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Fibularis longus</u><br><br>* <u>Tibialis posterior</u><br><br><br> |

Plantar aponeurosis and the medial longitudinal arch of the foot




### <u>Fascia</u> and retinacula of the foot




* Plantar fascia (<u>plantar</u> <u>aponeurosis</u>)

* A thick band of <u>connective tissue</u> that extends from the <u>calcaneal</u> tuberosity to the <u>plantar</u> aspect of the <u>proximal</u> <u>phalanges</u> of the toes

* Supports the bony arches of the foot

* Plays an important role in the dynamics of the foot

* Clinical significance: <u>plantar fasciitis</u>

* There are three main retinacula of the foot.





| Overview of foot retinacula |  |
| --- | --- |
| Retinacula | Characteristics |
| <br><u>Anterior</u> retinacula (extensor retinacula) | <br><br>* Superior <u>extensor retinaculum</u> of the ankle<br><br>* Thick transverse band of <u>fascia</u> that extends from the <u>anterior</u> surface of the <u>tibia</u> to the <u>anterior</u> surface of the <u>fibula</u><br><br>* <u>Tendons</u> of the <u>anterior compartment of the leg</u>, the <u>anterior</u> tibial vessels, and the <u>deep peroneal nerve</u> pass under it.<br><br>* Inferior <u>extensor retinaculum</u> of the ankle<br><br>* Transverse Y-shaped band of <u>fascia</u> that extends from the <u>medial malleolus</u> (upper arm of Y) and <u>plantar</u> <u>aponeurosis</u> (lower arm of Y) medially to the <u>lateral</u> aspect of the <u>calcaneus</u> (base of Y)<br><br>* <u>Tendons</u> of the <u>anterior</u> compartment pass under it.<br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Medial retinaculum</u> (flexor retinaculum of the foot; flexor retinaculum) | <br><br>* Description: a thick oblique band of <u>fascia</u> that extends from the <u>medial malleolus</u> to the <u>medial</u> aspect of the <u>calcaneus</u><br><br>* Function: <u>Tendons</u> of the deep <u>posterior</u> compartment, the <u>posterior</u> tibial vessels, and the <u>tibial nerve</u> pass under it.<br><br><br> |
| <u>Lateral</u> retinacula | <br><br>* Superior peroneal retinaculum: extends from the <u>lateral malleolus</u> to the <u>lateral</u> aspect of the <u>calcaneus</u><br><br>* Inferior peroneal retinaculum: a continuation of the <u>lateral</u> aspect of the inferior <u>extensor retinaculum</u><br><br>* Function: They hold the two <u>tendons</u> of the <u>lateral compartment of the leg</u> in place.<br><br><br> |
| Tarsal tunnel | <br><br>* Description: an osteofibrous channel bound by the <u>medial malleolus</u>, <u>talus</u>, and <u>calcaneus</u> at the deep aspect and the <u>flexor retinaculum of the foot</u> superficially<br><br>* Contents<br><br>* <u>Tibial nerve</u><br><br>* <u>Posterior tibial artery</u> and <u>vein</u><br><br>* <u>Tendon</u> of the <u>flexor hallucis longus</u><br><br>* <u>Tendon</u> of the <u>flexor digitorum longus</u><br><br>* <u>Tendon</u> of the <u>posterior tibialis</u><br><br>* Clinical significance: <u>tibial nerve</u> compression in <u>tarsal tunnel syndrome</u><br><br><br> |

## Muscles

### Muscles of the leg




* The <u>muscles of the leg</u> exert their action on the ankle, foot, and toes

* The deep <u>fascia</u> of the leg divides these muscles into three compartments  

* <u>Anterior</u> compartment

* Common nerve supply: <u>deep peroneal nerve</u>

* Common function: <u>dorsiflexion</u> of the ankle (extension)

* <u>Posterior</u> compartment (<u>superficial</u> and deep group)

* Common nerve supply: <u>tibial nerve</u>

* Common function: <u>plantarflexion</u> of the ankle (<u>flexion</u>)

* <u>Lateral</u> compartment

* Common nerve supply: <u>superficial peroneal nerve</u>

* Common function: <u>eversion of the foot</u>





![Osteofascial compartments of the leg](media/xg1r5yc19u1yj4p5k9r0zpyt.jpg)

Osteofascial compartments of the leg




#### Anterior compartment of the leg (extensor compartment)




| Characteristics of the <u>anterior</u> leg compartment |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Muscle | Origin | Insertion | Innervation | Function | <br>Testing <br> |
| Tibialis anterior | <br>* <u>Lateral</u> tibial condyle, <u>proximal</u> two thirds of the <u>lateral</u> surface of the tibial shaft, and the adjacent interosseous membrane<br><br> | <br>* <u>Medial</u> <u>cuneiform</u> and base of the 1<sup>st</sup> <u>metatarsal</u> bone<br><br> | <br>* <u>Deep peroneal nerve</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Ankle joint</u>: <u>dorsiflexion</u><br><br>* Foot: <u>inversion</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Foot <u>dorsiflexion</u> against resistance<br><br> |
| <br>Extensor hallucis longus (EHL) | <br>* Middle third of the <u>medial</u> surface of the <u>fibula</u> and the adjacent interosseous membrane<br><br> | <br>* <u>Dorsal</u> aspect of the base of the <u>distal</u> <u>phalanx</u> of the <u>hallux</u> (big toe)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Hallux</u>: extension<br><br>* <u>Ankle joint</u>: <u>dorsiflexion</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Hallux</u> extension against resistance<br><br> |  |
| <br>Extensor digitorum longus (EDL) | <br>* <u>Lateral</u> tibial condyle, <u>proximal</u> two thirds of the <u>medial</u> surface of the <u>fibula</u> and the adjacent interosseous membrane<br><br> | <br>* Divides into 4 <u>tendons</u> that insert into the bases of the middle and <u>distal</u> <u>phalanges</u> of the 2<sup>nd</sup>–5<sup>th</sup> toes<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Lateral</u> 4 toes: extension<br><br>* <u>Ankle joint</u>: <u>dorsiflexion</u> (weak)<br><br><br> | <br>* Extension of the <u>lateral</u> 4 toes against resistance<br><br> |  |
| Peroneus tertius | <br>* <u>Distal</u> third of the <u>medial</u> surface of the <u>fibula</u> and the adjacent interosseous membrane<br><br> | <br>* <u>Dorsal</u> aspect of the base of the 5<sup>th</sup> <u>metatarsal</u> bone<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Ankle joint</u>: <u>dorsiflexion</u> (weak)<br><br>* Foot: <u>eversion</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Cannot be tested in isolation<br><br> |  |

#### Posterior compartment of the leg (flexor compartment)




| Characteristics of the <u>posterior</u> leg compartment |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Group | Muscle |  | Origin | Insertion | Innervation | Function | Testing |
| <u>Superficial</u> flexor group | Triceps surae | Gastrocnemius | <br><br>* <u>Lateral</u> head: <u>lateral</u> femoral condyle<br><br>* <u>Medial</u> head: <u>medial</u> femoral condyle<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Tendons</u> of <u>gastrocnemius</u> and <u>soleus</u> fuse to form the <u>calcaneal tendon</u> (Achilles tendon) that is inserted into the <u>posterior</u> aspect of the <u>calcaneus</u> bone.<br><br> | <br>* <u>Tibial nerve</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Ankle: <u>plantarflexion</u><br><br>* Knee: <u>flexion</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Plantar flexion</u> of the ankle against resistance with the knee extended<br><br> |
| Soleus | <br>* Head of <u>fibula</u>, soleal line (a prominent, oblique ridge on the <u>posterior</u> surface of the <u>proximal</u> <u>tibia</u>), and middle third of the <u>medial</u> border of the <u>tibia</u><br><br> | <br>* Ankle: <u>plantarflexion</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Plantar flexion</u> of the ankle against resistance with the knee flexed<br><br> |  |  |  |  |
| Plantaris |  | <br>* <u>Lateral</u> supracondylar line of the <u>femur</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Calcaneus</u> bone<br><br> | <br>* Ankle: <u>plantarflexion</u> (weak)<br><br> | <br>* Cannot be tested in isolation<br><br> |  |  |
| Deep flexor group | Tibialis posterior |  | <br>* <u>Posterior</u> surfaces of the upper parts of the <u>fibula</u> and <u>tibia</u> and the adjacent interosseous membrane<br><br> | <br>* <u>Navicular bone</u>, intermediate <u>cuneiform bone</u>, and the bases of the 2<sup>nd</sup>–4<sup>th</sup> <u>metatarsals</u><br><br> | <br>* Foot: <u>Inversion</u> (main foot inverter)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Inversion</u> of the plantarflexed foot against resistance<br><br> |  |
| <br>Flexor digitorum longus<br>(FDL)<br> |  | <br>* <u>Posterior</u> surface of the <u>tibia</u><br><br> | <br>* Splits into 4 <u>tendons</u> that insert into the base of the <u>distal</u> <u>phalanges</u> of the <u>lateral</u> 4 toes<br><br> | <br>* <u>Lateral</u> 4 toes: <u>flexion</u> of the <u>distal</u> <u>phalanges</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Flexion</u> of the <u>lateral</u> 4 toes against resistance<br><br> |  |  |
| <br>Flexor hallucis longus<br>(FHL)<br> |  | <br>* <u>Distal</u> two thirds of the <u>posterior</u> aspect of the <u>fibula</u> and the adjacent interosseous membrane<br><br> | <br>* <u>Plantar</u> aspect of the base of the <u>distal</u> <u>phalanx</u> of the <u>hallux</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Hallux</u>: <u>flexion</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Flexion</u> of the <u>hallux</u> against resistance<br><br> |  |  |
| <u>Popliteus</u> |  | <br>* Tendinous origin from <u>knee joint</u> capsule and <u>lateral</u> femoral condyle<br><br> | <br>* <u>Posterior</u> surface of the <u>proximal</u> <u>tibia</u> (superior to <u>soleal line</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Internally rotates</u> the <u>tibia</u> on the <u>femur</u> (unlocking the fully extended knee)<br><br> | <br>* Cannot be tested in isolation<br><br> |  |  |

| <br>Peroneus longus (<u>fibularis longus</u>) | <br>* Head and <u>proximal</u> two thirds of the <u>lateral</u> surface of <u>fibula</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Lateral</u> aspects of the base of the 1<sup>st</sup> <u>metatarsal</u> and the <u>medial</u> <u>cuneiform bones</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Superficial peroneal nerve</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Ankle: <u>plantarflexion</u><br><br>* Foot: <u>eversion</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Tested together by everting the foot against resistance<br><br> |

### Muscles of the foot




* The <u>muscles of the foot</u> are divided into two groups based on where the muscle belly is located.

* Extrinsic <u>muscles of the foot</u>: muscle bellies are located in the leg (see “<u>Muscles of the leg</u>” above)

* <u>Intrinsic muscles of the foot</u>: muscle bellies are located within the foot

* <u>Dorsal</u> intrinsic muscles: innervated by the <u>deep fibular nerve</u>

* <u>Plantar</u> intrinsic muscles: innervated by branches of the <u>tibial nerve</u> (<u>medial</u> and <u>lateral</u> <u>plantar</u> nerves)

* Tested by asking the examinee to perform the action of the muscle against resistance

## Vasculature

### <u>Arteries</u> of the leg




| <br>Characteristics of <u>arteries</u> of the leg [[1]](/library/ES08Yf) |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Characteristic | Anterior tibial artery | Posterior tibial artery | <br>Fibular artery (<u>peroneal artery</u>) |
| Origin | <br>* A terminal branch of the <u>popliteal artery</u><br><br> | <br>* A terminal branch of the tibioperoneal trunk of the <u>popliteal artery</u><br><br> | <br>* A terminal branch of the tibioperoneal trunk of the <u>popliteal artery</u><br><br> |
| Course | <br><br>* Begins in the <u>popliteal fossa</u>, at the inferior border of the <u>popliteus muscle</u><br><br>* Enters the <u>anterior compartment of the leg</u> through a gap in the upper part of the interosseous membrane<br><br>* Lies on the interosseous membrane throughout its course<br><br>* Lies between the two malleoli at the <u>ankle joint</u><br><br>* Continues as the <u>dorsalis pedis artery</u> beyond the <u>ankle joint</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Begins in the <u>popliteal fossa</u>, at the inferior border of the <u>popliteus muscle</u><br><br>* Lies deep to the <u>soleus muscle</u> in the leg<br><br>* Passes deep to the <u>flexor retinaculum</u> and under the <u>medial malleolus</u><br><br>* Ends beyond the <u>medial malleolus</u> by dividing into <u>medial</u> and <u>lateral</u> <u>plantar</u> <u>arteries</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Begins in the <u>popliteal fossa</u>, ∼ 2.5 cm below the <u>popliteus muscle</u><br><br>* Travels along the <u>medial</u> border of the <u>fibula</u><br><br>* Ends at the inferior tibiofibular <u>joint</u> by dividing into <u>calcaneal</u> branches<br><br><br> |
| Branches | <br><br>* Recurrent branches to the <u>anastomosis</u> around <u>the knee joint</u><br><br>* Muscular branches<br><br>* <u>Medial</u> and <u>lateral malleolar</u> branches<br><br><br> | <br><br>* A circumflex branch to the knee<br><br>* Muscular branches<br><br>* <u>Medial malleolar</u> and <u>calcaneal</u> branches<br><br><br> | <br>* Muscular branches<br><br> |
| Supply | <br>* <u>Anterior</u> compartment of the leg<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Posterior</u> compartment of the leg<br><br>* <u>Plantar</u> aspect of the foot<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Lateral</u> and deep flexor compartments of the leg<br><br> |
| Important relations | <br>* Accompanied by the <u>deep peroneal nerve</u><br><br> | <br>* Accompanied by the <u>tibial nerve</u><br><br> | <br>* N/A<br><br> |

### <u>Arteries</u> of the foot [[1]](/library/ES08Yf)




#### Dorsum of the foot




##### Dorsalis pedis artery




* Origin: continuation of the <u>anterior tibial artery</u> beyond the <u>ankle joint</u>

* Course

* Travels in the 1<sup>st</sup> intermetatarsal space, <u>lateral</u> to the <u>tendon</u> of the EHL

* Passes through the 1<sup>st</sup> <u>dorsal</u> interosseus muscle and enters the sole

* Ends by <u>anastomosing</u> with the <u>lateral</u> <u>plantar</u> <u>artery</u> and giving off the 1<sup>st</sup> <u>dorsal</u> <u>metatarsal</u> <u>artery</u>

* The <u>dorsalis pedis artery</u> is often aberrant or absent.

* Branches

* Tarsal <u>arteries</u>

* Arcuate <u>artery</u>: gives rise to the <u>lateral</u> 3 <u>dorsal</u> <u>metatarsal</u> <u>arteries</u>, from which the digital <u>arteries</u> arise





![Dorsal arteries of the foot](media/v2t1f4bmqzetglplevo6wy0l.jpg)

Dorsal arteries of the foot




#### Sole of the foot




* Branches of the <u>posterior tibial artery</u>

* <u>Medial</u> <u>plantar</u> branch: supplies the <u>medial</u> side of the sole

* <u>Lateral</u> <u>plantar</u> branch: supplies the <u>lateral</u> side of the sole and <u>anastomosis</u> with the <u>dorsalis pedis</u>

* <u>Plantar</u> arterial arch

* Formed by the <u>anastomosis</u> between the <u>dorsalis pedis</u> and <u>lateral</u> <u>plantar</u> <u>arteries</u>

* Located on the <u>plantar</u> aspect of the bases of the <u>lateral</u> 4 <u>metatarsal</u> bones

* Branches: 4 <u>plantar</u> <u>metatarsal</u> <u>arteries</u>





![Plantar arteries of the foot](media/tcskbx9fqegckl99w7prhze8.jpg)

Plantar arteries of the foot




### Veins of the leg [[1]](/library/ES08Yf)




#### <u>Superficial veins</u>




The <u>superficial veins</u> lie within the <u>subcutaneous tissue</u>. There are two main <u>superficial</u> <u>veins of the leg</u>:




##### Great saphenous vein (<u>GSV</u>)




* Origin: continuation of the <u>medial</u> marginal <u>vein</u> of the foot (<u>medial</u> end of the <u>dorsal</u> venous arch)

* Course

* At the ankle: passes in front of the <u>medial malleolus</u>

* In the leg: ascends along the <u>medial</u> aspect of the shin

* At the knee: behind the <u>medial</u> condyles of the <u>femur</u> and <u>tibia</u>

* Thigh: <u>medial</u> aspect of the thigh

* Termination: saphenofemoral junction (<u>SFJ</u>)

* The site at which the <u>GSV</u> passes through the <u>saphenous opening</u> in the deep <u>fascia</u> of the thigh to meet the <u>femoral vein</u>.

* The position is fairly constant at 4 cm inferolateral to the <u>pubic tubercle</u>.

* Main tributaries

* <u>Short saphenous vein</u>

* <u>Superficial</u> external pudendal <u>vein</u>

* <u>Superficial epigastric veins</u>

* <u>Superficial</u> circumflex iliac <u>vein</u>

* <u>Lateral</u> femoral cutaneous <u>vein</u>

* Drains: the anteromedial aspect of the sole, leg, and thigh

* Important relations: <u>saphenous nerve</u> accompanies the <u>GSV</u> below the knee

* Clinical significance

* <u>Varicose veins</u>

* <u>Thrombophlebitis</u>

* Can be harvested for <u>vein</u> grafts for peripheral or coronary arterial <u>surgery</u>





![Saphenofemoral junction](media/oxdt4my7rdp57xq4p6gdkn6p.jpg)

Saphenofemoral junction




##### Small saphenous vein (SSV)




* Origin: continuation of the <u>lateral</u> marginal <u>vein</u> of the foot (<u>lateral</u> end of the <u>dorsal</u> venous arch)

* Course:

* At the ankle: passes behind the <u>lateral malleolus</u>

* In the leg: ascends in the midline of the calf towards the <u>popliteal fossa</u>

* Termination: saphenopopliteal junction (SPJ)

* The site at which the SSV drains into the <u>popliteal vein</u>

* Unlike the <u>SFJ</u>, the location of the SPJ is variable, lying within, <u>proximal</u>, or <u>distal</u> to the <u>popliteal fossa</u>.

* Important relations: <u>Sural nerve</u> accompanies the SSV through most of its course.





#### Deep <u>veins of the leg</u>




* The <u>deep veins</u> lie deep to the deep <u>fascia</u>.

* They accompany the <u>arteries</u> of the leg:

* <u>Anterior tibial veins</u>

* <u>Posterior tibial veins</u>

* <u>Fibular veins</u> (<u>peroneal veins</u>)

* These <u>deep veins</u> join at the inferior border of the <u>popliteus muscle</u> to form the <u>popliteal vein</u>.

* Clinical significance: <u>deep vein thrombosis</u>





![Veins of the leg (ventral aspect)](media/cb6dqkg5smjlovka5ruraf7i.jpg)

Veins of the leg (ventral aspect)

![Veins of the leg (dorsal aspect)](media/sf4kjbp3hxtvsoo0wsbu0ozc.jpg)

Veins of the leg (dorsal aspect)




### Veins of the foot [[1]](/library/ES08Yf)



* Digital <u>veins</u> (on the sides of the toes) → <u>metatarsal</u> <u>veins</u> (in the intermetatarsal spaces) → deep <u>plantar</u> venous arch (<u>plantar</u> aspect of the <u>lateral</u> 4 <u>metatarsal bones</u>) → <u>medial</u> and <u>lateral</u> <u>plantar</u> <u>veins</u> → <u>GSV</u> and SSV

## Innervation

### Motor and sensory innervation of the lower extremity




| Characteristics of motor and sensory innervation of the leg |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nerves |  | Origin | Motor supply | Sensory supply | Clinical significance |
| Mixed motor and sensory nerves | Tibial nerve | <br><br>* A terminal branch of the <u>sciatic nerve</u><br><br>* Arises at the apex of the <u>popliteal fossa</u><br><br>* <u>Nerve roots</u>: <u>ventral</u> divisions L4–<u>S3</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Posterior compartment of the leg</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Sural nerve</u> (see below)<br><br>* <u>Medial</u> <u>calcaneal</u> branch: <u>skin</u> over the heel (not shown in image)<br><br>* <u>Medial</u> <u>plantar</u> nerve: <u>medial</u> half of the sole (excluding the heel) and the <u>plantar</u> aspect of <u>medial</u> 3.5 toes<br><br>* Lateral plantar nerve: <u>lateral</u> half of the sole (excluding the heel) and the <u>plantar</u> aspect of the <u>lateral</u> 1.5 toes<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Tarsal tunnel syndrome</u><br><br>* <u>Tibial nerve injury</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Common peroneal nerve<br>(<u>common fibular nerve</u>) | <br><br>* A terminal branch of the <u>sciatic nerve</u><br><br>* Arises at the apex of the <u>popliteal fossa</u><br><br>* <u>Nerve roots</u>: <u>dorsal</u> divisions L4–<u>S2</u><br><br>* Course<br><br>* Travels along the <u>lateral</u> border of the <u>popliteal fossa</u><br><br>* Winds around the neck of the <u>fibula</u> where it terminates by dividing into the <u>superficial</u> and deep peroneal nerves<br><br><br> | <br>* None<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Lateral</u> sural cutaneous nerve (<u>lateral</u> cutaneous nerve of calf): <u>skin</u> over the <u>lateral</u> aspect of the leg<br><br>* Sural communicating nerve: joins the tibial part of the <u>sural nerve</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Common peroneal nerve injury</u> (e.g. fibular neck <u>fracture</u>, compression from <u>splint</u>)<br><br> |  |
| Deep peroneal nerve | <br><br>* A terminal branch of the <u>common peroneal nerve</u><br><br>* Arises at the neck of the <u>fibula</u><br><br>* <u>Nerve roots</u> L4–L5<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Anterior</u> compartment of the leg<br><br> | <br>* 1<sup>st</sup> web space of the foot (i.e., the <u>sandal gap</u>)<br><br> |  |  |
| Superficial peroneal nerve | <br><br>* A terminal branch of the <u>common peroneal nerve</u><br><br>* Arises at the neck of the <u>fibula</u><br><br>* <u>Nerve roots</u> L4–L5<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Lateral</u> compartment of the leg<br><br> | <br>* <u>Distal</u> part of the <u>anterior</u> aspect of the leg and the dorsum of the foot (except the 1<sup>st</sup> web space)<br><br> |  |  |
| Pure sensory nerves | Saphenous nerve | <br>* Branch of the <u>femoral nerve</u> that arises in the <u>femoral triangle</u><br><br> | <br>* None<br><br> | <br>* <u>Skin</u> over the <u>medial</u> half of the leg<br><br> |  |
| Sural nerve | <br>* Formed by the union of sural branches from the tibial and common peroneal nerves<br><br> | <br>* None<br><br> | <br>* <u>Skin</u> over the posterolateral aspect of the <u>distal</u> third of the leg and the <u>lateral</u> border of the foot<br><br> | <br>* <u>Sural nerve lesion</u><br><br> |  |





> [!NOTE]
> TIPPED = <u>tibial nerve</u> versus <u>peroneal nerve</u>
> <u>TIP</u> = Tibial nerve Inverts and Plantarflexes the foot → cannot walk on TIPtoes when injured
> <u>PED</u> = Peroneal nerve Everts and Dorsiflexes the foot → <u>foot drop</u> when injured

### <u>Dermatomal</u> distribution of the leg and foot




* <u>Anterior</u> leg

* <u>Medial</u> third: L4

* Middle third: L5

* <u>Lateral</u> third: <u>S1</u>

* <u>Posterior</u> leg

* <u>Medial</u> third: L4

* Middle third: <u>S2</u>

* <u>Lateral</u> third: <u>S1</u>

* <u>Dorsal</u> and <u>plantar</u> aspects of the foot

* <u>Medial</u> half: L5

* <u>Lateral</u> half: <u>S1</u>

## Clinical significance

* <u>Tibial fracture</u>

* <u>Medial tibial stress syndrome</u>

* <u>Fibular fracture</u>

* <u>Ankle sprain</u>

* <u>Ankle fracture</u>

* <u>Peripheral arterial disease</u>

* <u>Deep vein thrombosis</u>

* <u>Varicose veins</u>

* <u>Peripheral nerve injuries</u>

* <u>Plantar fasciitis</u>

* <u>Thromboangiitis obliterans</u>
